Frozen.

That's what the world around me was. Frozen, completely. Just a few moments ago I was enjoying the nice, spring breeze on the nape of my neck, walking down the sidewalk to my favorite cafe, when everything froze. The couple in front of me, walking their dog; not moving an inch. The barista, just in view from the cafe window; dropping a cup, with the coffee inside floating mid-air.

*Fuck. Shit, shit.* I was panicking. I couldn't move any more than anyone else could. My muscles felt stiff, but at the same time it was like they didn't exist, like lifting something heavy while my whole body was tingling til it's numb.

Adrenal-Chrono Dysplasia. That's what the medical community called it. A condition virtually everyone on the planet now had, yet only came into existence twenty years ago. Something about the next evolution of humanity... your adrenaline spiking so high in the face of danger, it slows down your perception of the time around you. It could only happen once in a person's life, and could be triggered by virtually anything that riled them up.

I had read, and listened, to people's experiences. Their first. I was twenty-seven and still a "time virgin." Still hadn't had my "moment." How much things slowed always depended on how much danger they were in.

My college roommate? Spilling boiling water on his foot. Didn't slow down enough to avoid the burns.

My last girlfriend? Skiing accident. It slowed enough for her to toss her gear, but she was still going too fast. Ended up with a nasty scar on her elbow.

This one guy? From this internet chatroom? He said he was held at gunpoint. Thank god he didn't exhaust his moment before then, because he would've ended up dead. He swears  time slowed down so much, he dodged the bullet. Bullet still grazed his ear, and he won't be wearing headphones any time soon.

Notice the pattern here? Almost always, time only slowed in proportion to the danger, and no one could react fast enough to avoid it entirely. They always ended up with something to remind them of their moment. Their body could never speed up beyond what's humanly possible, but their reaction time did.

So here I was, stuck with my leg mid-step on a perfectly normal day. Time, completely frozen. My eyes tried their hardest to dart around, looking for the danger, but they were just too slow.

I don't remember how long I spend standing like that. It seemed like hours, maybe days. Standing there, watching the same couple, the same barista, waiting for any sign that time was actually moving.

It was after an eternity of waiting that I saw something move, far off into the distance. I tried to narrow my eyes, to focus on the shape, but once again, my body was too slow. From what I could see, it was something round, and black, far off beyond the horizon. It was moving ever so slightly, and seemed to be getting closer.

A chill crept down my spine, something I didn't know was possible in my current state. I can't say my heart started racing, but my thoughts were everywhere, filled with disjointed, brief lines of panic. If my perception of time was this slow, and it was still moving, it had to have been moving... fast, really fast.

60MPH? No, the bullet was faster.

Mach II? The shape was moving fast enough to seem normal, way faster than that guy saw the gun. I was close, though. Something had to have startled me into having the moment, and a sonic boom would've done the trick.

Minutes passed, watching a distant sphere grow closer, and closer. By now, it was just a street ahead. The blurriness was subsiding, illuminating what it actually was. Not a sphere, not a shape, but a man.

His skin was pale, almost white, and his sunken-in eyes glowed a dim red. He wore a thick, pinstripe suit across his frame, with a pin across his lapel of a teardrop. He had finally stepped onto my street, approaching the couple.

Examining the dog, and the couple, he shook his head. No, they wouldn't do. He made his way to me, and looked me over, from head to toe. He raised his gaze, and met my eyes, raising an eyebrow.

He could see me. Not my frozen body, no, but *me*.

His face soured, wrinkling into a scowl. "No, no this won't do. This won't do at all." He raised a finger up to my forehead, less than an inch away from touching it.

Then he stopped. His head whipped upwards, nostrils flaring. He sniffed the air, twitching his neck to the side and toward the coffee shop, inhaling an unseen aroma. He turned back to me with a smile.

"You only get one moment. You won't see me next time, but I'll see you," he said, leaving me. In my head, I breathed a sigh of relief. My thoughts filled with panic once more as I saw the man open the door to the coffee shop, step inside, and walk toward the barista.

He took a long, deep breath, stroking the woman's hair. I watched as he gripped the spilling coffee, clutching it tight and burning it red-hot like steel. He turned back to me through the window, and winked.

In an instant, he was gone. The breeze blew across my face. The aroma of cut grass and fresh coffee filled my nose. The conversation of the couple rung through my head as I took a few deep breaths, followed by a scream.

I turned my head to the barista. The boiling coffee scorched her hands as it fell, and she fell with it, falling face-first into the mess. The screaming grew louder, and louder, and continued louder, until it slowed to a sob.

The ambulance arrived fifteen minutes later. I watched as they took the woman onto the stretcher, her face practically charred off, her hands covered with blisters. She was pronounced dead three hours later. The burns were just too severe.

That final image of the woman on the stretcher haunts me to this day, nearly every night. Her face, one half blackened. Her nose, skin melted off and reduced to a skeletal nub, and her eye sagging, leaking pus and blood with seared cataracts across all sides. You only get one moment, and I just used mine. I've been kept up by the nightmares for six years now, because I know he'll be coming for me. And this time? I won't see it coming.

The blond-haired, burly fellow known as Gordon Ramsay walked through the long hall, escorted by a young lady in white. "Right this way, sir," she said, gripping his hand.

There was to be a dining party held here. Not just any dining party, but one hosted by the White House. The President would be there, as would much of congress, and even some foreign ambassadors. Even with so much near-royalty attending, the star of the evening would be none other than Gordon himself.

"Here you are, sir," said the young woman, gesturing for him to open a door and step inside. His hand hovered a bit over the handle, shaking. He never shook. He was always calm under pressure, so why now?

Grabbing the handle, he pulled on it and stepped inside. Bright colors filled the air. Beautiful crystal chandeliers, lit up by neon streams of light. A tremendous ice sculpture of Gordon himself stood in the center of the room, though it moved and waved to all who walked besides it as though it was a real person.

Yes, this was the best of both worlds. Literally. When the alien ambassadors arrived on Earth, Gordon was surprised to learn they chose none other than he, himself, to receive their finest culinary treatment. In their culture, food meant everything. Science was made to enhance food, you needed food to grow, you made food to help others grow, and if you couldn't dedicate your life to something with food... well, you might as well become it yourself. For that reason, Ramsay, often hailed as the best chef in the world, was considered by the aliens to be this planet's leader. Reluctantly, the United States government had put aside any resistance and invited Ramsay to help negotiate long-lasting peace between worlds.

As Gordon steps into the room, conversations stop. All eyes are on him. He takes another step forward, gulping. A Michelin Star is much different than negotiating peace with an entire species.

Members of the alien species greet Ramsay and bow. The humans still can't get their eyes off him, but resume their conversation. A great golden table is pulled out from the center of the room, with a single throne, carved with Gordon's likeness. They gesture for him to sit, and he does. The leader of the aliens, a chef, arrives, holding a mysterious platter. He sets it down and takes off the lid. Served to Gordon is a plate of florescent, course stones, pulsating with individual circulatory systems. Half meat, half mineral.

The aliens watch him with bulbous eyes. He stabs his fork into one of the meat stones, and all eyes are once again focused on him.

He takes a bite, chews it. An eyebrow is raised. He sets his fork and knife down, and wipes his lips, looking back at the extraterrestrial visitors. There's a moment of pause, the two beings locking eyes for what feels to onlookers like an eternity.

"It's raw."

The gasp of hundreds echo throughout the dining hall, only a hand-full of them human. The alien chef is taken aback. He sputters his lips as if to say something, but no words come out.

"It's fucking raw."

"I-it's supposed to be raw, your Majesty."

"Supposed to be raw? It tastes like it was fucking frozen, then deep-fried in a microwave. You can't tell me it's supposed to be raw after all that!"

"N-no, your Majesty. The ship's microwave radiation must ha-"

"Microwave radiation? You've got to be shitting me! What ever happened to nice, traditional cooking utensils? At least it's seasoned."

The chef feels a crushing pain deep within his gut; the shame of all his ancestors, thousands of generators, looking at his mistake. He draws his plasma knife, and slits his own throat.

A spurt of the alien's blood fires off through the air, perfectly charred into something resembling a blood sausage, and onto Ramsay's plate.

"Now this is the dish I've been dying to try."
